sections.heading: Seeing my need and Christ’s fullness
sections.text:
God, you have been teaching me that I do not have life, wisdom, holiness, or strength stored up in myself. I am needy, and pretending otherwise only leaves me emptier.

But everything I lack is found in Jesus. He is not full only for himself; he is full for his people. In him there is true knowledge for my blindness, grace for my sin, righteousness for my guilt, and life for my emptiness. Teach me to stop searching myself for what only Christ can give.
theological_themes: Christ’s fullness as the source of grace, righteousness, knowledge, and life
Christ’s fullness given for his people

scripture_references.connection: Paul says the fullness of deity dwells bodily in Christ and that believers have been filled in him. This directly grounds the prayer’s movement from personal lack to sufficiency found in Christ.
John presents Christ as the one from whose fullness his people receive grace. This supports the prayer’s claim that the believer’s supply is not self-generated but received from Christ.

sections.heading: Coming to Christ with empty hands
sections.text:
So when I feel my emptiness, help me not to run away from you or try to fix myself first. Draw me to Christ with open hands. Let me receive what is mine in him—not as something I earned or produced, but as something he holds for me and gives to me.

Let faith bring me out of the shallows and into the sea of Christ’s abundance, like a fish finally back in the water. When I am trusting him, I am not trapped in my own small resources. I am living in the wide place of what he has already provided.
theological_themes: Faith as receiving Christ and his benefits
Union with Christ as the believer’s access to Christ’s riches

scripture_references.connection: Jesus invites the thirsty to come to him and drink, and John connects this with the Spirit given to believers. The passage supports the prayer’s image of needy faith receiving life from Christ.

Paul prays that believers would be strengthened by the Spirit, rooted in Christ’s love, and filled with God’s fullness. This reflects the prayer’s desire to enter more deeply into what is already given in Christ.

sections.heading: Receiving the Spirit in Christ, not apart from him
sections.text:
Keep me from treating the Holy Spirit as if he were a separate power or experience I could take apart from Jesus. I do not want a gift while ignoring the Giver. I want to find Christ, drink from Christ, be filled with Christ—and in that way know the fullness of the Spirit.

Make me humble enough to be filled. Make me empty of self-confidence, self-righteousness, and self-reliance, so that your Spirit may have room to work in me. Give me the kind of faith that makes grace alive—faith that strengthens me, steadies me, and fills me with joy in you.
theological_themes: The Spirit’s work is inseparable from Christ
Faith as the way the believer receives the Spirit’s fullness
Humility and self-emptying before God’s grace

scripture_references.connection: Paul reminds believers that they received the Spirit by hearing with faith, not by works of the law. This supports the prayer’s emphasis that fullness comes through faith in Christ rather than self-achievement.

Stephen is described as full of faith and of the Holy Spirit. This illuminates the original prayer’s link between faith and fullness of the Spirit without turning the Spirit into an impersonal possession.

sections.heading: Being settled and assured in Christ
sections.text:
Father, root me deeply in Christ. Settle me there. Let my life be anchored in him so that I am not always looking elsewhere for security, worth, or peace.

Assure me that what is in Christ is truly given to me by grace. Let that certainty fill my heart—not with pride, but with joy and peace. Help me delight more in what I receive from him, and even more in him as the fountain of every good thing you give.
theological_themes: Joy and peace flowing from faith
Delighting in Christ above his benefits

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers to continue in Christ, rooted and built up in him. This supports the prayer’s request to be established and settled in Christ rather than living from instability or self-reliance.
Paul connects faith with joy, peace, and the power of the Holy Spirit. This closely matches the prayer’s final request for assurance that fills the heart with joy and peace.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original says faith comes first, then fullness of the Spirit. Taken too rigidly, that could sound as though faith is produced independently of the Spirit. I rendered it as the believer receiving and experiencing the Spirit’s fullness through faith, consistent with Galatians 3, without denying the Spirit’s prior work in bringing a person to faith.

The original warns against receiving the Spirit as a ‘thing’ apart from Christ. I preserved this because it is theologically important: the Spirit is personal and his ministry is inseparable from the Son, not an impersonal power to be acquired.
significant_interpretive_choices: The phrase about Christ’s fullness being ‘as mine, as if I had it in myself’ was rendered as receiving what is truly given in Christ, not as self-generated possession. This preserves assurance and union with Christ while avoiding the implication that the believer becomes independently sufficient.
I kept the original fish-and-sea image in modern form because it is concrete and central to the prayer’s picture of moving from self-contained emptiness into the abundance of Christ.

The repeated ‘Thou hast taught me’ structure was reshaped into a direct personal prayer so it sounds natural today, while retaining the progression: God teaches personal emptiness, Christ’s fullness, faith’s receiving, the Spirit’s filling, and settled assurance.
